newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek police clash with youths after Athens march.
newsitem.headline: Greek police clash with youths after Athens march.

text.p: Greek riot police fired tear gas on Sunday to disperse about 70 youths hurling stones in central Athens after a peaceful march marking the 23rd anniversary of a student revolt against the ruling military junta of the day.

Police said they quickly dispersed the youths with volleys of tear gas and returned to their positions around the Athens Polytechnic, where a revolt against the junta which ruled from 1967 to 1974 was crushed with tanks.
A group of self-styled anarchist youths gathered around the Polytechnic after the march, shouting slogans against the police and the press.
"Two attempts to climb the school's fence were thwarted by Polytechnic guards, with no police intervention," a senior policeman said.
He said riot police moved in only after the youths set fires near the Polytechnic and started to throw stones. The clash lasted less than five minutes.
Shortly before the incident, a gas-bomb attack against the State Scholarship Foundation in the Plaka area of Athens damaged the door to the building, he said.
A group called "Children of November" claimed responsibility for the attack and police said it was probably an attempt by anarchists to draw police away from the Polytechnic.

About 5,000 demonstrators earlier marched through Athens to the American embassy to commemorate the bloody uprising which helped bring down the U.S.-backed dictatorship. At least 20 students died but many historians put the number much higher.

Police on hand to prevent possible violence outnumbered the demonstrators by around three to one. They said the unusually heavy number of men around the capital was meant to head off any attemps by rioting youths to take over the Athens Polytechnic.
After last year's march, hundreds of youths describing themselves as anarchists occupied the school, set fire to it and caused considerable property damage.
Police arrested 470 youths after two days of clashes and more than 100 of them were given jail terms for taking part in the riots.
The November 17 march is usually peaceful but self-styled young anarchists often rampage through central Athens after it is over.
